about.certainty_rule: green = established (known science, or a defined / proved result in Maths); orange = leading idea / partial progress; red = unknown / open problem. A link takes the colour of its less-certain end.

about.what_this_file_holds: Earth from space to the inner core: atmosphere layers, ocean, crust, mantle and core, with real depths in km.
about.how_to_use: Every item has id, title, certainty, summary, details and sources (title, url, type). Full source details (year, link check) are in sources_used. A link's reason_sources are the sources on its two cards. Fact-check against the sources; flag anything that looks wrong or out of date.

planet.title: Earth
summary: Radius about 6,371 km. Mass about 6 × 10²⁴ kg.
Formed about 4.54 billion years ago.
details: Drawn as a cut-away: real layers to scale, shapes simplified (land on the left half, ocean on the right).

sources.title: Dalrymple 2001: The age of the Earth in the twentieth century: a problem (mostly) solved (Geological Society, London, Special Publications)

planet.title: Exosphere
summary: From about 600 km up to about 10,000 km.
Gas so thin its atoms hardly ever meet.
details: Its outer edge is fuzzy; it fades into space (some count it out to the Moon).

sources.title: NOAA JetStream: Layers of the Atmosphere

planet.title: Thermosphere
summary: From about 85 to 600 km up. Auroras glow here.
The ISS flies here, about 400 km up.
details: Thin gas can reach 2,000 °C, but it would feel cold: too few atoms to warm you.

sources.title: NOAA JetStream: Layers of the Atmosphere

planet.title: Mesosphere
summary: From about 50 to 85 km up.
Most meteors burn up here.
details: The coldest part of the atmosphere, about −90 °C at the top.

sources.title: NOAA JetStream: Layers of the Atmosphere

planet.title: Stratosphere
summary: From about 12 to 50 km up.
Holds the ozone layer, which blocks most UV light.

sources.title: NOAA JetStream: Layers of the Atmosphere

planet.title: Troposphere
summary: From the ground up to about 12 km (8 km at the poles, 18 km at the equator).
Almost all weather happens here.
details: Holds about three quarters of the air’s mass.

sources.title: NOAA JetStream: Layers of the Atmosphere

planet.title: Atmosphere
summary: A thin layer of gas: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen.
Zoom in to see its 5 layers.
details: Half of all air is below about 5.5 km.

sources.title: NOAA JetStream: Layers of the Atmosphere

planet.title: Kármán line
summary: 100 km up: a common agreed edge of space.
It is a convention, not a physical wall.

sources.title: McDowell 2018: The edge of space: Revisiting the Karman Line (Acta Astronautica)

planet.title: Space Station (ISS)
summary: Orbits about 400–420 km up.
Goes round Earth about every 90 minutes.
details: Shown far bigger than real (it is about 109 m wide).

sources.title: NASA: Space Station Facts and Figures

planet.title: Ocean
summary: Covers about 71% of Earth. Average depth about 3.7 km.
Deepest point: about 10.9 km (Challenger Deep).

sources.title: NOAA Ocean Service: How deep is the ocean?

planet.title: Oceanic crust
summary: About 7 km thick, mostly basalt.
Young: rarely older than about 200 million years.
details: Made at mid-ocean ridges and sinks back into the mantle.

sources.title: White et al. 1992: Oceanic crustal thickness from seismic measurements and rare earth element inversions (J. Geophys. Res.)

planet.title: Continental crust
summary: About 35 km thick on average, up to 70 km under big mountains.
Lighter granite-like rock; parts are over 4 billion years old.
details: Its base is the Moho, where rock gets much denser.

sources.title: Christensen & Mooney 1995: Seismic velocity structure and composition of the continental crust: A global view (J. Geophys. Res.)

planet.title: Crust
summary: Earth’s thin rocky skin: less than 1% of its volume.
Zoom in to see ocean and continent crust.

sources.title: Christensen & Mooney 1995: Seismic velocity structure and composition of the continental crust: A global view (J. Geophys. Res.)
White et al. 1992: Oceanic crustal thickness from seismic measurements and rare earth element inversions (J. Geophys. Res.)

planet.title: Upper mantle
summary: From the crust down to about 410 km. Solid rock (peridotite).
It flows very slowly, a few cm a year, moving the plates.
details: The plates (lithosphere) are the stiff top ~100 km; below is the softer asthenosphere.

sources.title: Dziewonski & Anderson 1981: Preliminary reference Earth model (Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors)

planet.title: Transition zone
summary: From about 410 to 660 km down. Minerals squeeze into new forms.
It may hold a lot of water inside minerals (how much is still debated).
details: A diamond found in 2014 held ringwoodite with water, from this zone.

sources.title: Dziewonski & Anderson 1981: Preliminary reference Earth model (Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors)

planet.title: Lower mantle
summary: From about 660 to 2,891 km down. Hot solid rock.
Its main mineral, bridgmanite, is the most common mineral on Earth.
details: Two continent-sized blobs sit at its base; where they came from is unknown.

sources.title: Dziewonski & Anderson 1981: Preliminary reference Earth model (Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors)

planet.title: Outer core
summary: From about 2,891 to 5,150 km down. Liquid iron and nickel.
Its flow makes Earth’s magnetic field.

sources.title: Dziewonski & Anderson 1981: Preliminary reference Earth model (Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors)

planet.title: Inner core
summary: A solid iron-nickel ball, radius about 1,220 km.
About 5,000–5,400 °C, near the Sun’s surface temperature.
details: It is solid because of the huge pressure.
Its age is debated: roughly 0.5–1.5 billion years.

sources.title: Dziewonski & Anderson 1981: Preliminary reference Earth model (Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors)
